lines.text: Here are two real pieces of code doing the identical job on the identical pile of records. One just reaches into each record directly. The other makes a fresh copy of it first, for no real reason, before doing the identical work.
Does that extra, needless copy show up in how fast each one gets through the whole pile?
Barely at all.
Both of them land in essentially the same, real range, close enough that the difference isn't the story here.
Run it for real: both versions tear through millions of records a second, landing close enough to each other that nobody would call one of them meaningfully faster.
Now measure the identical pile of records a completely different way: not how fast, but how much real memory each one actually reaches for, record by record.
Does that number stay just as close as speed did, or does something else show up?
Something else shows up.
The version that copies each record reaches for a dramatically larger pile of real memory, record after record.

Run it for real: the version that reaches in directly barely touches memory at all, a handful of bytes per record, while the version that copies first reaches for roughly a whole record's worth, every single time.

lines.text: Put those two real numbers side by side: a handful of bytes against something far closer to a whole record's worth, for work that ran at essentially the identical speed.
Is that a small difference, or a real, structural one?
A real, structural one.
More than twenty times the real memory, for work that looked, by speed alone, like it cost the identical amount.
Run it for real: the copying version reaches for more than twenty times the real memory the direct version does, for the identical speed and the identical final result.
One real, well-known piece of documentation, about the single place every real memory request in a running program actually goes through, describes exactly this in its own words.
One real allocator stands behind every single real request the whole program makes, reached only through a few shared functions, never called by hand.

So here's what both of these real runs were really showing: two pieces of code can look identical by speed alone and still be paying a dramatically different real price underneath, every single time they run.
Speed alone told half the story, the half everyone already thinks to check. Watching what something actually reaches for told the rest of it.

And that's really the whole real lesson this domain keeps coming back to: build it so it holds up, watch it closely enough to actually know, and never trust just one number to tell you the whole real story.
